title: Judith Butler
summary: Judith Butler (born 1956) is an American philosopher, one of the key figures of poststructuralism, known for the theory of gender performativity. After 2001, vulnerability, grief and nonviolence move to the centre of Butler's thinking: what it means to live while depending on one another, and whose lives society recognizes as worthy of being mourned.
onEmotions: Butler thinks about feelings through relationships: from the very beginning we depend on others — on their care, their gaze, their language — and so strong feelings lay bare what we are made of. Grief, passion and rage take us "beside ourselves": in these states it becomes clear that the "I" is not an autonomous fortress but a knot of ties. Butler calls this openness to injury, shared by all living beings, precariousness, and its unequal distribution in society precarity. Another important idea is "frames": society determines in advance whose losses are noticed and whose grief is recognized — that is, which lives are "grievable." For Butler, vulnerability is not a weakness to be hidden but the ground of ethics and solidarity.

anxiety.text: Anxiety often speaks of something very real: we are vulnerable, and there is much in life we cannot fully protect ourselves from. Judith Butler makes this fact not a reason for panic but the basis of a philosophy. In Precarious Life, Butler writes that vulnerability is a condition shared by all living beings: the body is open to the world, depends on others, can be injured. Butler criticizes the fantasy of total invulnerability: the attempt to rule out risk once and for all often leads only to more tension and to closing ourselves off from others. From this angle, your anxiety is not a mistake but a sense of this openness. You don't have to defeat it; you can share it, acknowledging that others are vulnerable too — and that this is exactly why we need one another.
anxiety.practice: Think about who else in your life might be feeling a similar vulnerability. What changes in your anxiety when you imagine that it isn't only yours?

fear.text: Fear is a legitimate response to the fact that we can be harmed. After the events of September 11, 2001, Judith Butler reflected on what society does with fear. It can make us build walls, divide people into "us" and "them," and seek safety by making others the vulnerable ones. Butler proposes another path: to acknowledge that precariousness is shared by all, even though it is distributed unequally (this unequal distribution is what Butler calls precarity). For you, this may mean that fear doesn't have to separate you from people. It can instead become a point of understanding: others get scared too, and all of us can be hurt. Fear recognized as shared isolates less and connects more — and becomes easier to carry.
fear.practice: Name exactly what you are afraid of. Then ask yourself: who else besides me knows this fear?

sadness.text: Sadness sometimes comes with no obvious cause — and still has every right to be there. In The Psychic Life of Power, continuing Freud's thinking on melancholia, Judith Butler writes about losses that could not be openly acknowledged and mourned: attachments that those around us didn't consider "acceptable," possibilities we had to give up in order to meet expectations. Such unlived losses, for Butler, don't disappear — they settle inside as a quiet sadness. From this angle, your sadness may hold the memory of something you lost but were never able to name. This is not weakness but a kind of faithfulness. Sometimes it helps simply to allow the thought: perhaps I am sad about something I was once not allowed to mourn.
sadness.practice: Write: "Perhaps I'm sad about…" — and keep going without picking your words, even if it's something people "aren't supposed" to be sad about.

grief.text: Grief is one of the deepest experiences, and Judith Butler believes it reveals the truth about who we are. In Precarious Life, Butler writes that in losing another, we realize they were part of us, that our "I" is woven out of ties. That is why grief knocks us off course: what disappears is not only the person but also part of who you were with them. Butler doesn't call for "getting over" grief and returning to how things were. Mourning, for Butler, is agreeing to undergo a change whose outcome cannot be known in advance. Another important idea is "grievability": the right of every life and every loss to be mourned. Your grief deserves recognition, however others may judge it.
grief.practice: Think about which part of you was bound up with the one (or the thing) you lost. Acknowledge it with tenderness.

quote.text: Perhaps mourning has to do with agreeing to undergo a transformation (perhaps one should say submitting to a transformation) the full result of which one cannot know in advance.
quote.author: Judith Butler

loneliness.text: Loneliness is agonizing, and there is an important truth in that agony. For Judith Butler, a person is not a separate fortress from the start: we come into the world completely dependent on others — on their care, voice, gaze — and our "I" takes shape out of these ties. That is why loneliness hurts so much: it feels not like a lack of something extra but like a wound in the very foundation. Butler calls this original embeddedness in relationships relationality: we exist only in our ties with others. From this angle, loneliness is not proof that you are unneeded but a sign that you are made for connection. It speaks the language of need, and needing others is, for Butler, not a weakness but a shared condition of human life, one that unites us rather than divides us.
loneliness.practice: Think of a person — or a voice from a book or film — thanks to whom you once felt like yourself. What did you receive from that connection?

anger.text: Anger is a legitimate feeling, especially when it responds to injustice. In The Force of Nonviolence, Judith Butler doesn't demand that rage be suppressed. On the contrary, Butler acknowledges that aggression is part of human life and asks: what are we to do with it? The answer is nonviolence — understood not as passivity or "good behaviour" but as an active, sometimes very intense practice: holding your rage in a form that doesn't destroy your ties with others and with yourself. Butler starts from the premise that we are all interdependent: by harming another, we also undermine our own world. From this angle, your anger can be a force — not the kind that smashes, but the kind that insists, refuses to be silent, and demands justice.
anger.practice: What form could you give your anger so that it is heard, but without wounding you or others? Write down one sentence you would like to say.

shame.text: Shame burns because it touches the very core: as if you were not the person you "should" be. Judith Butler shows that many such "shoulds" are not nature but norms that are repeated so often that they start to seem natural. Butler calls this idea performativity: gender, for example, is not an inner essence but something we constantly perform, in response to expectations. Shame often arises where we don't fit such norms. But if norms are created by repetition, they are not final — they can be repeated differently. From this angle, your shame speaks not of your being "wrong" but of a collision with a frame that is too narrow. You can ask yourself: whose norm is this, and does it have to be mine?
shame.practice: Put into words the norm you feel ashamed of not meeting: "People are supposed to…" Where did it come into your life from?

guilt.text: Guilt can matter: it shows that you care how your actions have affected others. In Giving an Account of Oneself, Judith Butler reflects on how we answer for our actions. Butler notes that we can never fully explain ourselves: our "I" has been shaped by relationships and a history we didn't choose and don't fully understand. Butler calls the demand — made of oneself or of another — for absolute transparency and flawless consistency "ethical violence." This doesn't remove responsibility, but it changes its tone: you can answer for an act while acknowledging your own limits. Then guilt becomes not endless self-accusation but a turning toward the other — a readiness to say "I'm sorry" and to hear what mattered to them.
guilt.practice: Write a short, honest account of what happened in three sentences — and add: "I can't fully understand myself, and that is also true."

envy.text: Envy is unpleasant to notice in yourself, but it is very human. Judith Butler writes almost nothing directly about envy, but it can be seen through a theme that is central for Butler: recognition. Butler's first book was devoted to Hegel and his idea that a person desires recognition — wants to be seen and affirmed by others. Butler adds that we don't set the conditions of recognition: society decides in advance which lives, achievements and bodies "count." From this angle, one could say that envy is often not about the thing itself but about recognition: the other person seems to have received the affirmation you are lacking. This helps you treat envy more gently: behind it is a normal need to be seen. And you can ask yourself who already truly sees you, and how.
envy.practice: What in someone else's life seems to you to be "recognized," while in yours it isn't? Name one person who already sees you.

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy can be heavy precisely because they are hard to explain. In Undoing Gender, Judith Butler asks: what makes a life livable? Butler's answer is that it is not only a matter of willpower. A person needs recognition, support, connections and material conditions; without them life wears thin, even if everything looks fine from the outside. In later work, Butler stresses that no body can sustain itself alone — we all rely on others and on the world around us. From this angle, one could say that emptiness can be a sign that your supports have grown few, not that you have "forgotten how to feel." This shifts the question: not "what's wrong with me?" but "what am I missing right now in order to live more fully?"
emptiness.practice: Ask yourself: what one support — a person, a place, a familiar ritual — would make today a little more livable?

confusion.text: Confusion is the state in which familiar answers stop working, and that can be frightening. Judith Butler opens their best-known book, Gender Trouble, with the thought that trouble and turmoil are not necessarily bad. They arise when stable categories — who I am, how to live "properly" — begin to waver. For Butler, such moments open up a possibility: what seemed natural turns out to have been made, and so it can be otherwise. In Giving an Account of Oneself, Butler also shows that a person is never fully transparent to themselves. From this angle, confusion is not a failure but an honest encounter with the fact that you are larger than any ready-made definition. Within it, you don't have to hurry toward answers.
confusion.practice: Which definition of yourself — "I'm the kind of person who…" — has been shaken right now? What might be opening up behind it?

quote.text: Perhaps trouble need not carry such a negative valence. […] trouble is inevitable and the task, how best to make it, what best way to be in it.
quote.author: Judith Butler

fatigue.text: Tiredness and burnout are not a sign of weakness but often an honest signal from the body. In Notes Toward a Performative Theory of Assembly, Judith Butler writes that a body never holds itself up on its own — it needs food, rest, shelter, care, other people, working systems of support. When supports are few and demands keep growing, strength inevitably runs out. Butler distinguishes between the vulnerability we all share and precarity — the unequal distribution of these supports in society. From this angle, your tiredness is not only a personal story. Perhaps you are expected to hold on alone where any human being needs support. Acknowledging this dependence is not humiliating but freeing: needing rest and help is a normal human condition.
fatigue.practice: List what you are leaning on right now to keep going. Which one support are you missing — and where could you find at least a little of it?

boredom.text: Boredom can be wearing: the days all look alike, and nothing catches your interest. Butler doesn't write about boredom directly, but from the standpoint of the theory of performativity one could say this. For Butler, our life is largely made up of repetitions — gestures, roles, habitual ways of being ourselves. These repetitions sustain norms, but freedom is hidden in them too: no repetition is ever an exact copy, and in the gaps between them the possibility of doing things differently appears. Boredom may be the feeling of a repetition that has become mechanical. But it is also a hint: since your life is made of repetitions, each one holds a small chance of a shift. You don't have to change everything — you can perform something familiar a little differently and see what changes.
boredom.practice: Choose one habitual action today — a route, a phrase, a ritual — and repeat it a little differently. Notice what changes as you do.

joy.text: Joy is a wonderful feeling, and it needs no justification. Judith Butler writes that in strong experiences — grief, rage, passion — we find ourselves "beside ourselves." Butler recalls the literal meaning of the word "ecstasy": the Greek ek-stasis means "standing outside oneself." Joy, too, takes us beyond our own boundaries: we dissolve into music, into a conversation, into a shared movement. In later work, Butler also reflects on the power of people gathered together — on how, alongside others, something arises that no one has alone. From this angle, your joy is not only a personal pleasure but also a sign of connection: for a moment you stopped being a separate "I" and became part of something larger. You can simply accept this with gratitude.
joy.practice: Recall a moment of recent joy: when were you a little "beside yourself"? What or whom were you connected with then?

love.text: Love and tenderness make us open — that is their strength and their risk. For Judith Butler, this is not a flaw but the very essence of human relationships. In Precarious Life and Undoing Gender, Butler writes that we don't simply "have" ties with others — we are made by them, and in love, as in grief, this becomes obvious: another person is able to change us, to knock us out of our habits, to make us different. Butler doesn't see this as a threat that must be controlled — rather, as the truth about how we are made. From this angle, tenderness doesn't make you weak; it shows that your boundaries are alive and permeable. Accepting love means agreeing that the other "undoes" you a little, and not being afraid of it.
love.practice: How has this person changed you — in your habits, your words, your view of the world? Name one such change.

quote.text: Let's face it. We're undone by each other. And if we're not, we're missing something.
quote.author: Judith Butler

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling in which it becomes visible that we don't manage alone. For Judith Butler, this is not a passing observation but the foundation of ethics: each of us lives from birth thanks to the care of others, and this interdependence doesn't end in adulthood. In The Force of Nonviolence, Butler stresses that lives are bound up with one another: we breathe the same air, rely on shared homes and roads, on the labour of countless strangers. From this angle, one could say that gratitude is the moment when we acknowledge our dependence without shame. It doesn't make us debtors; it shows that we are part of a web, and brings us back to the thought that every life in this web is valuable.
gratitude.practice: Think of one stranger whose work made your life a little easier today. Thank them in your mind.

hope.text: Hope can seem naive against the backdrop of hard news, but Judith Butler believes that without imagining a better world it is impossible either to live or to act. In The Force of Nonviolence, Butler invites us to imagine a world where all lives are equally "grievable," that is, equally recognized as valuable. Butler understands that this sounds unrealistic, and deliberately defends such imagining against the charge of naivety: what is called "realism" often merely entrenches existing injustice. From this angle, hope is not a denial of reality but a refusal to treat it as final. Your hope doesn't have to be certainty. It is enough that you allow for the possibility that the world — and your life — could be arranged differently.
hope.practice: Describe in one sentence what a slightly kinder world — or your tomorrow — could be like. Don't check whether it's "realistic."

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a longing for what shaped us, and there is a great deal of tenderness in it. In The Psychic Life of Power, Judith Butler writes about "passionate attachments": a child becomes attached to those it depends on before it can choose anything, and out of these early ties its "I" takes shape. From this angle, one could say that nostalgia is an echo of such attachments: to the people, places and voices that once made us who we are. Butler shows that these ties can be complicated — love and dependence are mixed in them. That is why nostalgia can be both bright and painful. It doesn't need to be taken apart completely. You can simply acknowledge: this is where I come from, and it still lives in me.
nostalgia.practice: Which person, place or sound from the past do you miss right now? What of it still lives in you?

craving.text: A sharp "I want it right now" can feel like a force that is impossible to resist — and there is no reason for shame in that. In The Psychic Life of Power, Judith Butler writes about "passionate attachment": a person can be deeply attached even to what subordinates them, because through that bond they once found a footing and a way to exist. From this angle, one could say that a craving is not simply weakness of will but an attachment in which an old need is hidden: for comfort, for relief, for a minute of not feeling vulnerable. Butler reminds us that vulnerability is a shared human condition, not a personal flaw. If you hear this need behind the craving, it becomes easier to wait out the wave with understanding for yourself: it rises, peaks and subsides.
craving.practice: When the craving rolls in, ask yourself: what feeling do I want to hide from right now? Name it in one word and watch how the wave changes.

addiction.text: When your life has long been organized around one thing, getting out of that circle seems almost impossible — and it is not a moral failure. Butler shows that we become ourselves through repetition: gender, habits and ways of living are not given but are something we perform again and again. This is performativity. From this angle, one could say that addiction also rests on repetition, which over time starts to feel like the very essence of a person: "this is who I am." But Butler's thought has a hopeful side: if something is created by repetition, it can be repeated differently — not in one leap, but through small shifts. Besides, for Butler no one lives alone: we depend on one another, and accepting support is not weakness but an ordinary human condition.
addiction.practice: Notice one moment in your day where the habitual repetition could be shifted slightly — not cancelled, but changed. If you'd like, talk about it with someone who understands, for example in a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: The morning after can be agonizing: your body hurts, your memory serves up fragments of last night, and anxiety and shame wash over you. In Giving an Account of Oneself, Butler shows that none of us can give a full account of ourselves: part of our life always remains opaque even to us. Usually this "opacity" seems like a reason for shame, but Butler draws a different conclusion: since we are not fully transparent to ourselves, ethics calls for leniency — toward others and toward ourselves. From this angle, gaps in memory and awkward recollections are not a final verdict on you. You can acknowledge that something went wrong yesterday without demanding flawless self-knowledge of yourself. Right now the most important thing is to take care of your body; sorting things out can come later.
hangover.practice: Say one sentence to yourself: "I don't know everything about myself — and that doesn't make me a bad person." Then do one simple thing for your body.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria, when everything seems possible, is a vivid and real experience. Butler describes strong feelings as states in which we are "beside ourselves" — literally taken beyond our own limits; hence the word "ecstasy," from the Greek ek-stasis, "standing outside." For Butler, this is not an anomaly but a laying bare of how we are made: our "I" is open to the world and to others and is never locked inside. From this angle, euphoria can be understood as a moment when this openness is felt especially keenly and joyfully. It doesn't need an explanation, and you don't need to look for a catch. You can simply notice what and whom you feel connected to in this moment — these connections, unlike the burst itself, can last a long time.
euphoria.practice: Notice whom or what you want to share this joy with. Write down a name or a word — let it stay after the burst.

crash.text: The comedown after a high can be abrupt: yesterday everything was shining, and today it seems grey and heavy. Butler reminds us that we are vulnerable and dependent beings: our state changes along with our body, our circumstances and other people. Strong highs take us "beside ourselves," and coming back inevitably feels like a fall. From this angle, one could say that the comedown is neither payback for joy nor proof that something is wrong with you, but the ordinary rhythm of a being that doesn't live in an invulnerable fortress. Butler often speaks of a "livable life": not one where everything is good all the time, but one that can be borne. On days like these it is worth leaning on what makes life livable: sleep, food, the people close to you.
crash.practice: Name one thing that makes life a little more livable today — hot tea, a call, a blanket. Allow yourself to have it.

panic.text: A panic attack is genuinely frightening: your heart pounds, you can't get enough air, a sense that something terrible is about to happen sweeps over you. Usually such a wave peaks and subsides within a few minutes. For Butler, a person is above all a bodily, vulnerable being: our openness to the world begins with the body, and the body can experience a threat before we have had time to understand anything. From this angle, panic is an acute experience of the precariousness that Butler considers common to all people, not a sign of some special weakness of yours. Butler also stresses that vulnerability is also the capacity to respond, to feel support and being held. In a moment of panic you can look for the simplest support: the floor under your feet, your own exhale, an object in your hand.
panic.practice: Press your feet into the floor and make your exhale longer than your inhale. Take any object in your hand and name three of its qualities.

dread.text: The question "what is all this for?" and the thought of finitude can open a real abyss beneath your feet. Butler speaks of precariousness: every life is fragile, and this is a condition shared by all living beings. But from this fragility Butler draws a conclusion not about meaninglessness but about connection: precisely because we are vulnerable, we need one another and can care for one another. The value of a life, for Butler, shows in its being "grievable" — that is, in how dear it is to someone and how much it is cherished. From this angle, existential dread touches on a truth — life is fragile — but not the whole truth. Fragility is also what connects you with others, and meaning lives precisely in these connections.
dread.practice: Name one being, person or place that is dear to you. Notice that this connection is part of who you are.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives while you are, once again, not there is exhausting and makes you compare constantly. Butler writes a lot about "frames": society determines in advance what counts as a visible, valuable, "real" life, and what stays out of the picture. From Butler's perspective, one could say that a social media feed is a frame too: it shows only selected scenes and quietly turns them into the norm. Your fear of missing out is a reaction not to other people's real lives but to a frame that makes some lives bright and others invisible. Your own ordinary life doesn't become any less real because of it. You can ask yourself who built the frame in which you suddenly find yourself "not there," and how — and what was left outside its edge.
fomo.practice: Describe in two sentences a scene from your life that nobody would post to a feed, but that is dear to you.

sleepless.text: At night, when you can't sleep, thoughts become louder and more merciless, and morning seems endlessly far away. Butler reminds us that a person is not a self-sufficient fortress: we are vulnerable, and during the day we are held up by many invisible ties — conversations, tasks, the presence of others. At night these supports recede, and the precariousness shared by all people is felt more keenly. From this angle, night-time anxiety is not proof that everything really is bad, but a laid-bare experience of your own vulnerability in the silence. Butler sees vulnerability not as a verdict but as the ground of solidarity. You could also put it this way: at this very hour, others somewhere are also awake, with similar thoughts. You are not alone in this sleeplessness, even if it is dark and quiet around you.
sleepless.practice: Put your palm on your chest and feel it rise and fall. In your mind, wish a good night to everyone else who is also awake right now.

betrayal.text: Betrayal is a wound inflicted where you were open. Butler writes that from the very beginning we depend on others and are therefore open not only to care but also to injury: the same openness that makes love possible makes pain possible too. In Precarious Life, Butler shows that vulnerability cannot be eliminated — we can only choose how to respond to it. After a betrayal you want to close yourself off forever, but the dream of total invulnerability, for Butler, leads to hardening rather than to safety. From this angle, your pain doesn't prove that trusting was foolish. You can allow yourself anger and grief, take time to recover, and still not give up the openness you are made of.
betrayal.practice: Write one sentence about what you feel toward the person who betrayed you, without softening it. Then one about what you want to keep in yourself.

jealousy.text: Jealousy takes hold of you completely: the fear of losing, the wish to hold on, shame at that wish. Butler writes that in love and desire we are "undone" by each other: the other becomes part of our "I," and so the threat of losing them feels like a threat to ourselves. From this angle, jealousy is not an ugly weakness but a painful testimony to how connected you are with the other. But Butler also insists on the "opacity" of every person: the other can never be fully known, let alone be our property. That is exactly why an encounter with them is possible at all. You can acknowledge jealousy without turning it into control: ask yourself which part of your "I" feels threatened, and take care of that part first.
jealousy.practice: Finish the sentence: "When I'm jealous, the part of me that's afraid is the part that…" Ask how you can support it without controlling the other person.

resentment.text: An old grudge is like a burden you carry for years, and it has a right to exist: behind it is real pain. Butler, continuing Hegel's line of thought, writes a lot about recognition: we vitally need to be seen and to have our pain acknowledged. From this angle, resentment often lasts so long because the harm was never acknowledged — neither by the one who caused it nor by those around. It keeps the truth about what happened when nobody else is keeping it. In The Force of Nonviolence, Butler reflects on how to break cycles of retaliatory harm without denying the harm itself. You don't have to forgive or forget. You can acknowledge what happened yourself — give yourself the recognition others didn't give — and then the resentment may become a little lighter.
resentment.practice: Write one sentence you would like to hear from the person who hurt you. Read it aloud to yourself.

heartbreak.text: A breakup can feel as if you have been taken apart. Butler describes this almost literally: in love we are "undone" by the other, and when they leave, we lose not only them but also the part of ourselves that existed alongside them. That is why after a breakup it is hard to understand who you are now. Butler doesn't suggest quickly "pulling yourself together": to grieve is to agree to a change whose outcome cannot be known in advance. And one more thing: loss, for Butler, not only isolates but also connects — almost everyone knows this pain, and in it you are not alone. From this angle, a broken heart is not a defeat but a testimony to how deeply you are able to connect with others.
heartbreak.practice: Think of someone who also went through a breakup and went on living. What would that person say to you now?

quote.text: Loss has made a tenuous "we" of us all.
quote.author: Judith Butler

impostor.text: The fear of being found out any minute makes every success fragile. Through the idea of performativity, Butler shows that many of our identities — even gender — are not a hidden essence inside but something we perform over and over. From this angle, one could say that a professional role works the same way: there is no "real" expert hidden somewhere deep inside, only repeated actions out of which the role is made. Then the feeling "I'm only pretending" doesn't expose you — it merely notices how all roles are made. Those who look confident are performing their roles too; they just doubt them less. Your performance is not a fake: skill and competence are also born of repetition. You are not deceiving others; you are taking part, like everyone else.
impostor.practice: Write down three things you have already done many times in your role. That is your competence — made of repetitions.

self_hatred.text: The inner critic can speak so cruelly that its voice seems like the voice of truth. But it isn't. In The Psychic Life of Power, drawing on Freud and Nietzsche, Butler describes how conscience forms when external demands and reproaches turn inward — and a person begins to treat themselves the way they were once treated. The critic is not your essence but an internalized voice of power that over time came to sound from within. In Giving an Account of Oneself, Butler adds that no one can know themselves fully, so ethics calls for leniency, including toward yourself. From this angle, the critic's verdict is not the last word. You can listen to it without agreeing, and notice whose tone it speaks in.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one phrase of your inner critic and ask: whose voice was this once? Then rewrite it in the tone of someone who is kind to you.

quote.text: If we speak and try to give an account from this place, we will not be irresponsible, or, if we are, we will surely be forgiven.
quote.author: Judith Butler

helplessness.text: Feeling powerless to change anything is a heavy experience, and it often rests on reality: there are circumstances stronger than any one person. Butler distinguishes between precariousness, shared by everyone, and precarity — the unequal distribution of vulnerability, in which some people are far less protected than others. From this angle, your helplessness may be not a personal weakness but an honest reaction to conditions that really do constrain you. But Butler doesn't stop there. In The Force of Nonviolence and other works, vulnerability is understood as what connects people: where no one can manage alone, people act together. One person's helplessness is not the same as the powerlessness of many. Even admitting "I can't do this alone" is already a step toward connection.
helplessness.practice: Name one person with whom you could share this burden, even if only by talking. You don't need to decide anything — just name them.

procrastination.text: "I can't get started" is a state in which it is easy to start gnawing at yourself. Butler's thinking can be applied like this: in every task we are not only acting but also performing a norm — of the "productive," "responsible" person — and this performance is expected to be flawless. Performativity, for Butler, is never perfect: we always repeat norms with deviations, glitches, hesitations. From this angle, one could say that putting things off is one such glitch: resistance to a demand that feels too heavy or alien. This doesn't make the task unnecessary, but it changes your view: you are not "broken"; you have run into a norm that presses on you. You can ask whose measure this is — and begin not with a perfect performance but with an imperfect one.
procrastination.practice: Do the most imperfect version of the first step — a clumsy draft, a single line — and let it be bad.

uprooted.text: Moving or emigrating takes away not only your home but also the web in which you were recognized. Butler stresses that our "I" rests on recognition: we become ourselves in the eyes of others, in language, in familiar roles. In a new place this web is torn — nobody knows you, your language sounds foreign, your familiar ways of being yourself don't work. Hence the feeling of having lost your ground. Butler also writes about "dispossession": we never fully belong to ourselves and always depend in part on others. This knowledge is bitter, but there is hope in it too: since the "I" is created in ties, it can grow again in new ones. From this angle, roots are not only the past left back there, but also the ties that are slowly being woven here.
uprooted.practice: Recall one moment in the new place when you were recognized or called by your name. Write it down — this is the first thread.

overload.text: An endless stream of news and feeds can bring you to the feeling that your head is about to burst. In Frames of War, Butler shows that everything we see has been selected and shaped in advance by frames: some lives and events end up at the centre, others outside the picture. From this angle, a feed is an enormous machine of frames, and it demands that you respond to everything at once: grieve, be outraged, rejoice every few seconds. Your overload is not an inability to "take the hit" but the natural limit of a feeling being. Butler values an attentive, slow response to another. Stepping out of the stream doesn't mean becoming indifferent: sometimes it is the only way to truly notice even one person or one story.
overload.practice: Close the feed and choose one story from what you saw today. Think about it for a minute — only about it.

unreality.text: The feeling that the world, or you yourself, is somehow unreal can be very unsettling, and it deserves to be spoken of gently. Butler doesn't write about this experience directly, but from Butler's perspective one could say this: the sense of reality is not born in solitude. We feel real when we are recognized — when someone responds, names us, knows us. For Butler, the "I" is not a closed fortress but an interweaving of relationships; when the threads loosen, or life passes under heavy strain, reality can lose its density. From this angle, unreality is not proof that you "aren't there," but a signal of a lack of response. Reality can come back through simple things: someone's voice, touching an object, your own name spoken aloud.
unreality.practice: Say your name out loud and name three sounds you can hear right now.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare moment when you seem to forget yourself. Butler describes strong states as "ecstatic" in the original sense of the word: we find ourselves "beside ourselves," taken beyond our own limits. Butler usually speaks of this in relation to grief or passion, but from this angle the same can be said of awe. Awe is not a loss of self but a reminder that you have been open to the world and to others from the very beginning, that your "I" doesn't end at the boundary of your skin. This experience doesn't need to be analyzed or justified. You can simply let it last — and notice how, within it, the usual pressure to be separate and self-sufficient disappears.
awe.practice: Stay another minute with whatever filled you with awe. Notice where the boundary of your "I" lies at this moment — and whether there is one.

relief.text: Relief is the moment when tension finally lets go and your body exhales before you even realize it. Butler reminds us that we are vulnerable, bodily beings who are always bearing something: uncertainty, waiting, dependence on circumstances and on others. Relief makes visible how much strength went into that bearing. From Butler's perspective, one could say that relief often comes not only from within but also thanks to others: someone helped, something was resolved, the world turned out to be a little kinder. So in relief there is also gratitude to the ties that hold us. There's no need to hastily devalue it with worry about the future. You can give yourself time to feel: things have become easier right now, and that is true.
relief.practice: Note who or what helped this relief come about. If you'd like, say thank you to that person.

calm.text: Calm is a state in which you need neither to defend nor to prove anything. Butler writes a lot about how norms demand constant performance from us: to be the "right" kind of worker, partner, person. These demands sound almost all the time, even when we don't notice them. From this angle, one could say that calm is a rare pause in this endless performance: a moment when no role requires confirmation. For Butler, a "livable life" is a life in which you can breathe without being under constant threat. Your calm is a small embodiment of such a life. It doesn't need to be justified by productivity or earned. You can notice it and let it be — even for a few minutes.
calm.practice: Ask yourself: which role do I not need to perform right now? Spend a minute without it.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is the feeling that a new possibility has opened up and you want to bring it to life. Butler gives possibility enormous importance: for people hemmed in by norms, the mere appearance of another way to live, speak or be can change everything. Performativity, for Butler, means that we are not doomed to repeat the same thing: every repetition holds a chance of a shift. From this angle, inspiration is the experience of such a shift from within, the moment when you see that things can be otherwise. Butler also reminds us that we never create alone: language, images and other people's voices pass through us. You can cherish inspiration as a gift that came from your connections — and not demand immediate perfection from it.
inspiration.practice: Write down, in one sentence, the possibility that has just opened up. Don't plan — just record that "it could be otherwise."

quote.text: Possibility is not a luxury; it is as crucial as bread.
quote.author: Judith Butler

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude — secret joy at someone else's failure — is something almost nobody admits out loud, although probably everyone has felt it. Butler doesn't write about this feeling directly, but it can be seen through Butler's key idea of precariousness: each of us is vulnerable, can make mistakes, lose, stumble. Living with this knowledge is hard, and, in Butler's view, people and whole societies often try to push vulnerability outward — to attribute it to "others" so as to feel invulnerable themselves. From this angle, one could say that schadenfreude is a brief breather: the failure happened to someone else, not to me. This is not a verdict on your character; rather, it is a sign of how hard it is to carry your own fragility. If you acknowledge that everyone is vulnerable, someone else's failure can turn from relief into recognition.
schadenfreude.practice: Recall whose failure recently pleased you, and ask yourself: which of my fears did it touch? Write that fear down in one word.

contempt.text: Contempt is hard to admit: it seems arrogant, although underneath it there is often hurt, tiredness or fear. In Bodies That Matter (1993), Butler plays on the double meaning of the English word "matter" — as material and as having significance — and asks how society decides whose lives and bodies "matter" and whose don't. Such a division, for Butler, is not natural: it is created by norms that we all absorb, often without noticing. From this angle, one could say that contempt is a moment when this sorting kicks in within us and someone ends up "lower." The feeling itself is not a verdict on you, but it is worth questioning. Whose norm is it protecting? And what about this person stings you so much that you want to put them beyond the line? Sometimes behind contempt lies your own pain that was never given room.
contempt.practice: Finish the sentence: "This person seems not to matter, because…" Read it and ask: whose norm is this — mine, or one I've absorbed?

disgust.text: Disgust is a strong bodily "no": to a person, a situation, sometimes to your own body or actions. It arises quickly and seems natural. Following Julia Kristeva, Butler uses the concept of the "abject" — what we push away in order to draw the boundaries of our own self: the dirty, the alien, the "wrong." For Butler, these boundaries are not given by nature; they are maintained by constant rejection — and are therefore always a little shaky. From this angle, disgust is the work of a boundary: this is how the psyche protects what it takes to be itself. This is useful to know about self-disgust too: sometimes we push away in ourselves what others once called "unacceptable." Disgust doesn't need to be suppressed. But you can ask: which boundary is it guarding right now — and do I need that boundary in this form?
disgust.practice: Name what disgusts you and add: "This isn't me, because…" Look at the answer: whose voice can you hear in it?

revenge.text: The desire for revenge is understandable: you were hurt, and everything inside you demands that it not go unanswered. In Precarious Life, written after the attacks of September 11, 2001, Butler reflects on how quickly grief and pain turn into a thirst for retribution — in individuals and in whole societies. Butler doesn't deny anger, but suggests staying with the grief itself and not rushing to "resolve" it with a retaliatory blow. Revenge promises to restore the lost control, as if you could become invulnerable again. But for Butler, a wound reveals the truth of shared vulnerability, and a wound in return doesn't cancel it. From this angle, your desire for revenge is a signal of how deep the pain is and of an injustice that needs to be named. It can be given a voice — in words, in a demand for justice — without causing harm.
revenge.practice: Before you think about a response, write down: what exactly was taken from me, or hurt in me? Allow yourself to grieve that first.

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at the people closest to you — a partner, parents, children — is one of the most shameful feelings, and yet one of the most ordinary. In The Force of Nonviolence (2020), Butler draws on the psychoanalyst Melanie Klein: love and aggression, for Klein, are intertwined from the very beginning, because we depend most of all on precisely those we love. Dependence gives birth to both tenderness and rage. Butler draws an important conclusion from this: nonviolence is not the absence of aggression but a practice of dealing with it, the skill of holding it so that it doesn't destroy the bond. From this angle, your anger doesn't cancel your love and doesn't make you a bad parent or partner. It says that you feel cramped, burdened, or that something is missing. You can acknowledge it — and express it in words, not in an action that wounds.
anger_at_loved.practice: When the anger rises, pause and name it to yourself: "I'm angry, and I love." Then ask: what am I missing right now?

ambivalence.text: Loving a person and at the same time not being able to stand them is a hard combination, but a very common one. In The Psychic Life of Power, Butler shows that from childhood we become attached to those we depend on — and this attachment is inevitably passionate and ambivalent. Butler calls it "passionate attachment": a child cannot help loving those who care for it, even if that care is sometimes hard. Hence, in adult life, the mixture of tenderness and protest, gratitude and the wish to pull away. From this angle, your ambivalence is not a sign that something is wrong with love, but an honest trace of the dependence we are all made of. You don't have to choose one feeling and renounce the other. You can let them sit side by side and see what each is saying.
ambivalence.practice: Write two sentences that begin the same way: "I'm attached to this person because…" and "I find it hard with this person because…" Both can be true.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, a departure, or the death of a gravely ill loved one often comes together with shame: how can you feel lightness if you love them? Butler writes about grief as a state that resists full control and clarity. Following Freud, Butler notes that when we lose a person, we don't always know what exactly we have lost along with them — loss is enigmatic even to ourselves. Much can come together in it: love, tiredness, release from long tension, mourning for the life that existed before the illness or the discord. From this angle, relief is not betrayal but one of the threads in the complex fabric of grief. Grief changes us unpredictably, and there is no "correct" set of feelings you are supposed to have. Love and relief can exist together.
guilty_relief.practice: Write down all the feelings you have right now in a single list, without ranking them: love, relief, sadness, tiredness… Let them stand side by side.

indifference.text: Sometimes you look at someone else's grief or at an important event — and inside it is quiet. Then it becomes frightening: do I really not care? In Frames of War (2009), Butler shows that our feelings are never born in a vacuum: what moves us and what doesn't is largely determined by "frames" — the ways stories and images are presented, selected and repeated. Butler writes that our very affects are regulated: some losses are framed so as to evoke mourning, others so that they pass us by. From this angle, your indifference is not proof of heartlessness but, perhaps, the trace of a frame, or tiredness from the constant stream. Butler adds that frames are not airtight: they have cracks through which feeling unexpectedly breaks through. You can wait for such a moment without demanding it of yourself.
indifference.practice: Recall the "frame" in which you learned about the event: a headline, a short video, a retelling. How would the feeling change if you heard the story of one particular person?

escape.text: The wish to drop everything — your job, your city, your role — can be very strong. This is not about leaving life, but about wanting to live differently. One of Butler's main questions is: what makes a life "livable"? In Undoing Gender, Butler writes that the norms we live by can both sustain us and squeeze us to the point of the unbearable. A role — the good employee, the model parent, the reliable person — also rests on repetition. And since it is repeated, it can be repeated a little differently: that is performativity as Butler understands it. From this angle, the wish to escape is a signal that some norm has become too tight, not a whim. You don't have to tear everything down at once. You can find where, in the daily "performance" of your role, you could make a small shift.
escape.practice: Write down one habitual "line" of your role — something you do because "that's how it's supposed to be." How could you perform it tomorrow at least a little more in your own way?

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone unavailable or to the "wrong" person often comes unbidden and unsettles you. Butler passes no moral verdicts on desire — and neither will we. Butler's first book, Subjects of Desire (1987), is about how French philosophers read Hegel: in this tradition, desire is not just "I want" but a movement by which the "I" goes beyond itself and seeks itself in another. Later, Butler shows that society marks out in advance which desires count as "intelligible" and acceptable. From this angle, one could say that an attraction that is "not allowed" is not evidence of corruption but a sign that desire is always wider than the frames assigned to it. Deciding what to do with it is not the task of this minute. You can simply ask: what in me is this desire reaching for — what freedom, aliveness, new self?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down who you become in your imagination when you're with this person. Which quality of this "new self" do you especially need right now?

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgment is familiar to many: your body tenses, your words get stuck. This is not weakness but sensitivity to the fact that you are open to other people's gaze. In Giving an Account of Oneself, Butler writes that we become ourselves by being "addressed": others speak to us, name us, wait for a reply — long before we have chosen anything. That is why judgment stings so much: it touches the very foundation of the "I." But Butler adds something important: no one is fully transparent to themselves, and no one can present themselves flawlessly. This is a shared condition, not your personal shortcoming. From this angle, awkwardness among people is not a failure but an honest expression of the opacity everyone has. Others are most likely more preoccupied with their own anxiety than with yours.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, tell yourself: "I don't have to be fully understandable — to others or to myself." Notice how your body responds to this.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is exhausting: it's unclear what will happen, and there is nothing to lean on. Butler suggests seeing it not as a malfunction but as a shared condition of life. We don't own the future, because we live in dependence on others, on circumstances, on the world — this is precariousness. In Giving an Account of Oneself, Butler writes that ethics asks us to risk ourselves precisely in moments of unknowingness, when what formed us diverges from what lies before us. Not knowing, for Butler, is not only a threat but also a place where change and a new connection with others become possible. From this angle, uncertainty doesn't have to be "defeated"; it can be borne — and better together. You don't need to know everything in advance to take the next step.
uncertainty.practice: Write: "I don't know what will happen with…" — and next to it, add the name of someone with whom you could share this not-knowing. Maybe it's worth messaging them.

waiting.text: Waiting — for an answer, results, news — is hard because almost nothing depends on you. Butler helps you see this not as personal helplessness but as an expression of the fact that life is always partly in the hands of others. In Frames of War, Butler writes that precariousness means living among others: our fate depends on the decisions, care and actions of people we sometimes don't even know. Waiting lays this dependence bare especially sharply. But Butler doesn't consider it humiliating: it is the ground of solidarity, since others depend on us in just the same way. From this angle, your restlessness is an honest reaction to the fact that you don't control everything. While the waiting lasts, you can turn your attention to the part of life that really is in your hands right now — and to those who are waiting beside you.
waiting.practice: Make two columns: "what is in other people's hands right now" and "what is in mine." Choose one small task from the second column for today.

quote.text: Precariousness implies living socially, that is, the fact that one's life is always in some sense in the hands of the other.
quote.author: Judith Butler

regret.text: Regret — about something said, done or left undone — can come back again and again. In Giving an Account of Oneself, Butler shows that we can never give a full account of ourselves: much in us was formed before we could choose, by other people and by circumstances, and we are not transparent even to ourselves. Yet when we look back, we judge our past selves as if we had known then everything we know now. Butler doesn't remove responsibility but understands it differently — not as a demand for flawlessness, but as a readiness to answer to others while acknowledging our own limits. From this angle, your regret shows that you care, and that is valuable. And a simple thought can soften it: back then, you acted with the knowledge and the strength you had.
regret.practice: Write a short letter to yourself at the moment you regret: "Back then you didn't know…" End it with the words a kind friend would say.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is a pain with a name and a face. In Giving an Account of Oneself, Butler turns to the thought of the Italian philosopher Adriana Cavarero: the most important question between people is not "what are you?" but "who are you?" Each person is unique, and their story truly comes together only when someone else sees it and can tell it. A person close to you is someone who knows your story and holds on to it. That is why longing runs so deep: you miss not only their presence but also the one who saw you in exactly that way. From this angle, your longing is not weakness but a recognition of their uniqueness and of your bond. It doesn't need to be "let go" on command. You can let it live in memory and in the stories you tell about them.
longing.practice: Write a short story — a single scene — about how this person was when they were with you. A story can be kept and reread.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — for those suffering from war, disaster, injustice — can be almost unbearable, especially when the news comes in a continuous stream. Butler makes this pain a central theme of philosophy. In Frames of War, Butler asks: which lives do we recognize as "grievable," that is, worthy of being mourned? And answers: every life deserves mourning — regardless of country, language or side. From this angle, your pain is neither weakness nor "excessive sensitivity," but the capacity to recognize the value of the lives of people you have never seen. Butler doesn't suggest carrying it all alone: mourning, for Butler, connects people and can become the ground of solidarity. You can allow yourself to grieve — and look for those with whom this pain can be shared.
world_pain.practice: Allow yourself a minute of silence for those you are thinking about — without news or a screen. Then talk about it with someone who also cares.

rejection.text: Rejection hurts because it touches one of our deepest needs — to be recognized. Butler shows that this need is not a whim: we exist as social beings only insofar as someone recognizes us. But Butler also stresses something else: the conditions of recognition are not set by us, nor by any one person. In Undoing Gender, Butler writes that these conditions are created by society and change over time — they shape ideas about who "fits," who is good, attractive or successful "enough." When you are rejected, it is often just such a norm at work, not some deep knowledge of you. From this angle, rejection is an event within particular frames, not a final verdict on your worth. The pain of it is real. But it doesn't have the last word on who you are.
rejection.practice: Write down the "norm" by which you may have been judged. Then write one quality of yours that this norm is unable to see.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned has its roots at the very beginning of life: an infant depends completely on others and would not survive without their care. Butler considers this original dependence not a childhood remnant to be outgrown but a permanent feature of human existence. In Precarious Life, Butler writes that from the very beginning we are given over to others — before we are able to choose anything. That is why the threat of losing someone close resonates so deeply: it touches the very foundation. From this angle, your fear is not "excessive attachment" but the memory of a fundamental vulnerability shared by everyone. Butler suggests not being ashamed of dependence but widening its circle: we are held not by one person but by many ties — friendship, communities, mutual care. These can be noticed and strengthened.
abandonment.practice: Write down the names of three people or communities you depend on in some way, besides the one you're afraid of losing. Send one of them a few words today.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love hurts in a particular way: the feeling is alive, but there is no answer. Butler writes that in love and desire we find ourselves "beside ourselves" — we are carried toward the other and are no longer quite the masters of our feelings. This is not a sign of weakness but a property of any passionate bond. Butler recalls the Greek word ekstasis — literally "standing outside oneself." When there is no answer, this openness is left without support, and it seems you gave yourself in vain. From this angle, one could put it differently: the capacity to go beyond yourself like this is valuable and not so common, and it doesn't vanish because this time it met no answer. Your love has already changed you. In time, this openness will find somewhere to flow.
unrequited.practice: Write down how this love has expanded you — what you saw, felt, learned about yourself. This stays with you whatever the answer.

humiliation.text: Humiliation burns especially fiercely because it strikes at your dignity and happens in front of others. In Excitable Speech (1997), Butler explores how words are able to wound: an insult, a contemptuous nickname, mockery act almost like a blow. Butler explains this by the fact that we exist in language — we are called, named, and through this we become ourselves. That is why a wounding word strikes deep. But Butler also offers hope: the speaker doesn't fully own their words; their meaning can be contested, rethought, turned around. Many hurtful names have, over time, been reclaimed by those they were meant to wound, and filled with new meaning. From this angle, humiliation speaks of the act of the one who humiliated you, not of who you are at heart. The last word about you does not belong to the one who humiliated you.
humiliation.practice: Write down the word or phrase that wounded you. Next to it, write what you yourself could say in reply — even if only on paper, in your own words.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body is familiar to a great many people, and it is not your fault. In Gender Trouble, Butler shows that much of what seems "natural" about the body and how it ought to be is created by the repetition of norms — again and again, until they start to look like nature. But what is created by repetition is not final: it can be repeated differently. In Precarious Life, Butler adds that the body never belongs only to us: from the very beginning it is open to the gaze, touch and care of others — and that is why it is so sensitive to other people's judgment. From this angle, your dissatisfaction is largely the voice of internalized norms, not the truth about you. You can notice your body not only as an object of evaluation but as what you live, feel and are connected with the world through.
body_shame.practice: When a critical thought about your body comes up, add to it: "…that's what a norm I've absorbed tells me." Then name one thing your body let you feel today.

illness.text: When your body lets you down, the familiar feeling that you can rely on yourself collapses. It is frightening and infuriating, and these feelings are legitimate. Butler suggests seeing the body's vulnerability not as a defeat but as a shared condition of life. We were never fully independent: from birth we need care, food, shelter, other people. Illness merely makes this dependence visible. In The Force of Nonviolence, Butler writes about interdependence as what binds all living beings, not only "the weak." From this angle, needing help is nothing to be ashamed of: it is not a deviation from the norm of human life but its essence, which health temporarily hides. You can allow yourself to accept care without apologizing for it.
illness.practice: Name one thing you need help with right now, and one person you could ask. You can ask briefly and without explanations.

pride.text: Pride in what you have done is a good feeling, and you don't have to hide it behind modesty. Butler helps you see two sides to it. The first is action: for Butler, we are not simply "the way we are"; we become ourselves through what we do and repeat. What you have seen through is part of who you are becoming. The second side is connection: in Notes Toward a Performative Theory of Assembly (2015), Butler stresses that no one acts alone, and our ability to do anything rests on the support of others, on language, on infrastructure. From this angle, one could say that healthy pride doesn't contradict gratitude but complements it. You can take pleasure in your contribution — and notice those who made it possible. One doesn't diminish the other.
pride.practice: Write down what you are proud of, and below it — whom or what you'd like to thank for their support. Reread both parts with pleasure.

melancholy.text: Bright sadness is a quiet feeling in which grief sits alongside tenderness. It needs neither to be chased away nor to be cured. In The Psychic Life of Power, Butler draws on Freud, who observed that the "I" is largely made up of traces of those people and things we once loved and lost. Freud called the character of the ego a precipitate of abandoned attachments, and Butler develops this thought: losses don't disappear without a trace; they become part of who we are. From this angle, melancholy is a moment when these inner traces become audible: the past sounds in the present. This is not a breakdown or being stuck, but the memory of a love that goes on living in you. You can accept bright sadness as a quiet acknowledgment of what shaped you.
melancholy.practice: Name one loss or past period of your life whose trace you feel in yourself right now. What of it remains in you — a habit, a taste, an intonation?
